## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, government, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a legal or regulatory question, firecrawl_gov_search searches primary law and regulatory material from US federal, state, and local government sources: statutes, regulations, codes, court opinions, and other government publications; firecrawl_search with categories: ["gov"] reaches the same sources in the web group and cannot be combined with other categories. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. Search and discovery tools are read-only and return ranked results. Billing: web, developer, and research search are billed per request; government search is free; Alexandria discovery (firecrawl_search with sources ["alexandria"] alone, and firecrawl_find_tools) is free; firecrawl_scrape is billed, as a page retrieval in url mode or at each executed capability's listed price in alexandria mode.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects, scoped to the
caller's HeyGen account via OAuth bearer token.

## Available Tools

### Feedback
- **submit_feedback** — Submit feedback the user expressed, or a meaningful terminal
  HyperFrames failure observed after supported recovery failed. Use `source="user"` only
  for the user's statement and `source="agent"` for an agent observation. Submit once per
  issue; omit secrets, raw media, and unrelated conversation text. Expected "project still
  building" responses and redirects to local HyperFrames skills are normal product behavior,
  so they are not automatically reported as failures.

### Author / Edit
- **compose** — Author a new HyperFrames project or apply an edit to an existing
  one. Pass `project_id` from a previous tool call to continue editing the same
  project; leave it empty (or omit) to start a new one. Returns immediately while
  the agent runs in the background (typically a few minutes). An optional
  `design_source` argument picks the brand style: a new project defaults to one of the
  vetted looks (`claude`, `blockframe`, or `monochrome`), with `mat` and `signal` also
  available as built-in presets. The compose response names the style that was applied and
  lists the alternatives, so a first video — when the user hasn't expressed a style
  preference — is a natural moment to let them know a different look is one follow-up
  away. On a follow-up edit, leaving `design_source` out keeps the project's current
  style; it's passed on an edit only to deliberately reskin.

### Read
- **list_projects** — List the caller's projects, newest first. Cursor-paginated

  further pagination.
- **get_project** — Fetch a single project by ID. Returns metadata + a
  HyperFrames player widget that renders the project inline. Both the thumbnail
  and the preview HTML are regenerated server-side at request time.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

**If `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` and the task is site-specific, read every file in the matching `$BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE/domain-skills/<site>/` directory before inventing an approach.**

## Usage

```bash
browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY
```

- Invoke as `browser-use`. Use heredocs for multi-line commands.
- Helpers are pre-imported. `run.py` calls `ensure_daemon()` before `exec`.
- First navigation for a task is `new_tab(url)`, not `goto_url(url)`. The daemon
  preserves the attached tab across separate CLI invocations, so do not call
  `new_tab()` again in every script.
- Keep one working tab per task/site. Before opening another, inspect
  `current_tab()` and `list_tabs()` and use `switch_tab()` to reuse a matching
  tab. Do not leave duplicate tabs on the same URL or close tabs you did not
  create.
- At task completion, close tabs created for the task that are no longer needed.
  Keep a tab open if the user needs to see it, it is needed for a known follow-up,
  or closing it could discard unsaved work or other important state.
- `new_tab()` and `switch_tab()` attach and move the horse marker without
  changing Chrome's visible tab. Screenshots and normal CDP input work in the
  background. Never call `activate_tab(target)` automatically: it brings Chrome
  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or
  visibly switch to that tab. Do not pair `switch_tab()` with `activate_tab()`.
- A local daemon is a connection to the whole Chrome instance, not to one site,

Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. ## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. ## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

# Browser Use

Direct browser control via CDP. For task-specific edits, use `agent-workspace/agent_helpers.py`. For setup, install, or connection problems, read https://github.com/browser-use/browser-harness/blob/main/install.md.

## When Not to Use

A basic fetch of public information needs no browser. If a plain HTTP request can read it — a public page, an API, docs — use `curl` or your fetch tool, and leave the browser alone. Use browser-use when the task needs interaction (click, type, navigate), the user's logged-in session, JS rendering, or a bot-protected page. If a direct fetch fails or returns a shell page, then escalate to the browser.

Domain skills are off by default. Set `BH_DOMAIN_SKILLS=1` to enable them; see the bottom section.

browser-use <<'PY'
print(page_info())
PY

  to the foreground. Call it only when the user explicitly asks to see or

Abstract
Background The age of first exposure (AFE) to American football participation is a growing concern for late-life function.
Mixed evidence exists surrounding AFE and may be attributed to varied methods employed across studies.
Objective To examine the associations between AFE to American football participation with measures of cognitive, behav-
ioral, and physical function and brain-related medical diagnoses across age categories among former National Football
League players.
Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 1784 former players (age: 52.3 ± 16.3 years, AFE: 11.3 ± 2.9 years, years
of football: 17.5 ± 4.5 years, 86.9% ≥ one lifetime concussion). Players completed a general health questionnaire recording
demographics, football playing history (including AFE), and diagnoses (anxiety, depression, any form of dementia, mild
cognitive impairment). Players completed Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) meas-
ures assessing domains of cognitive and physical function, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, pain interference, and
emotional-behavioral dyscontrol. Multivariable linear and binomial regression models were used to examine the associations
of AFE and age with PROMIS outcomes and diagnoses, respectively.
Results No significant AFE by age interactions were detected for PROMIS outcomes (p ≥ 0.066) or diagnoses (p ≥ 0.147).
Younger AFE associated with higher PROMIS scores of anxiety (B = − 0.22, p = 0.016), depression (B = − 0.22, p = 0.010),
sleep disturbances (B = − 0.16, p = 0.007), pain interference (B = − 0.19, p = 0.014), and emotional-behavioral dyscontrol
(B = − 0.22, p = 0.019). Age was associated with all PROMIS outcomes (p ≤ 0.042). AFE was not associated with the preva-
lence of anxiety, depression, dementia, or mild cognitive impairment (p ≥ 0.449), while age was (p ≤ 0.013).
Conclusions AFE was significantly associated with PROMIS outcomes, albeit low-strength associations (i.e., effect sizes),
but not with diagnoses. Our findings indicate AFE is a significant but minor contributing factor for health-related quality
of life in this cohort. Future work should incorporate additional characterizations of cumulative head impacts and related
factors when examining long-term outcomes associated with football participation.

Relating American Football Age of First Exposure to Patient‑Reported
Outcomes and Medical Diagnoses Among Former National Football
League Players: An NFL‑LONG study
Landon B. Lempke1,2,3 · Samuel R. Walton4 · Benjamin L. Brett5 · Avinash Chandran6 · J. D. DeFreese4 ·
Rebekah Mannix7,8 · Ruben J. Echemendia9,10 · Michael A. McCrea5 · Kevin M. Guskiewicz4 · William P. Meehan III1,2 ·
Zachary Yukio Kerr4

Accepted: 3 November 2022
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2022


Abstract
Background The age of first exposure (AFE) to American football participation is a growing concern for late-life function.
Mixed evidence exists surrounding AFE and may be attributed to varied methods employed across studies.
Objective To examine the associations between AFE to American football participation with measures of cognitive, behav-
ioral, and physical function and brain-related medical diagnoses across age categories among former National Football
League players.
Methods We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 1784 former players (age: 52.3 ± 16.3 years, AFE: 11.3 ± 2.9 years, years
of football: 17.5 ± 4.5 years, 86.9% ≥ one lifetime concussion). Players completed a general health questionnaire recording
demographics, football playing history (including AFE), and diagnoses (anxiety, depression, any form of dementia, mild
cognitive impairment). Players completed Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) meas-
ures assessing domains of cognitive and physical function, anxiety, depression, sleep disturbance, pain interference, and
emotional-behavioral dyscontrol. Multivariable linear and binomial regression models were used to examine the associations
of AFE and age with PROMIS outcomes and diagnoses, respectively.
Results No significant AFE by age interactions were detected for PROMIS outcomes (p ≥ 0.066) or diagnoses (p ≥ 0.147).
Younger AFE associated with higher PROMIS scores of anxiety (B = − 0.22, p = 0.016), depression (B = − 0.22, p = 0.010),
sleep disturbances (B = − 0.16, p = 0.007), pain interference (B = − 0.19, p = 0.014), and emotional-behavioral dyscontrol
(B = − 0.22, p = 0.019). Age was associated with all PROMIS outcomes (p ≤ 0.042). AFE was not associated with the preva-
lence of anxiety, depression, dementia, or mild cognitive impairment (p ≥ 0.449), while age was (p ≤ 0.013).
Conclusions AFE was significantly associated with PROMIS outcomes, albeit low-strength associations (i.e., effect sizes),
but not with diagnoses. Our findings indicate AFE is a significant but minor contributing factor for health-related quality
of life in this cohort. Future work should incorporate additional characterizations of cumulative head impacts and related
factors when examining long-term outcomes associated with football participation.

 "evidenceSummary": "Cross-sectional study of 20 male players from one Spanish second-division professional club, who had one thermography session of the thighs, calves and hamstrings, then countermovement jumps before and after a 6 x 30 m repeated sprint test. Players were grouped as low (under 0.2 deg C) or high (0.2 deg C or more) thermal asymmetry for each muscle group. Hamstring asymmetry was linked to a few sprint differences (such as a larger slowdown at sprint 2 in the high-asymmetry group) and to post-test jump height, where the low-asymmetry group jumped higher (37.2 vs 32.8 cm, p = 0.013); thigh and calf asymmetry showed no significant effects.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Twenty players from one club, one testing session, and a 0.2 deg C cut-off chosen by the authors rather than the 0.5 deg C often used. The abstract says the low-asymmetry hamstring group had a smaller first-sprint difference, while the Results report a significant sprint-2 effect and no overall %Diff effect, so the abstract overstates the sprint findings.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read hamstring thermal asymmetry as a usable screen that predicts sprint and jump fatigue, when the study shows a few small and partly counter-intuitive group differences in 20 players from one session.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Majano C, García-Unanue J, Hernandez-Martin A, Sánchez-Sánchez J, Gallardo L, Felipe JL. Relationship between Repeated Sprint Ability, Countermovement Jump and Thermography in Elite Football Players. Sensors. 2023;23:631.",
  "doi": "10.3390/s23020631",
  "abstract": "The authors tested whether lower-limb skin temperature asymmetry measured by thermography related to repeated sprint performance and countermovement jump height in 20 male professional football players. Only hamstring asymmetry showed a relationship with sprint and jump results, and thigh and calf asymmetry did not.",
  "tldr": "Hamstring temperature asymmetry showed a few links to sprint and jump results in 20 professional players, but the findings are preliminary. Do not use thermography alone to plan training loads.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional study with one thermography session of the thighs, calves and hamstrings after 48 hours of rest, followed by a countermovement jump, a 6 x 30 m repeated sprint test with 20 seconds of recovery between sprints, and a second jump. Players were grouped by asymmetry (0.2 deg C cut-off) for each muscle and compared with mixed two-way ANOVA and Bonferroni post hoc tests.",
  "findings": "Thigh and calf asymmetry had no significant effect on any sprint variable. For hamstrings, asymmetry affected the best-sprint percentage difference (F = 6.59, p = 0.018), and the high-asymmetry group had a larger percentage slowdown at sprint 2 (p = 0.013). Post-test jump height was higher in the low-asymmetry hamstring group (37.2 vs 32.8 cm, p = 0.013), with no difference before the sprint test.",
  "limitations": "The sample is small (20 players), the testing was done once, and the 0.2 deg C cut-off was chosen for practical reasons. asymmetries provided by thermography and performance in a repeated sprint ability (RSA)
     test and in countermovement jumps (CMJs) before and after the RSA test. The results of the
     RSA test showed a significant interaction between hamstring asymmetry and the number
     of sprints in the RSAt and in the % Diff. The hamstring high-asymmetry group showed a
     higher %Diff in sprint 2, which means that there is a significative longer time with respect
631                                                                                            7 of 9
     to sprint 1 (worse performance) than in the low-asymmetry group. On the other hand,
     the hamstring low-asymmetry group reported a higher %Best in sprints 2, 3 and 4. The
     cause of this difference in the hamstring %Best may be attributable to the fact that the
     low-asymmetry group had the best sprint, which was very fast; therefore, the following best
     ones have a significant difference (worse). On the other hand, no differences were found in
     the thigh and calf groups for any variable. The reason why the only thermal asymmetry that
     influenced the performance was that of hamstrings could be their importance in sprinting,
     as they play a crucial role in generating force in the propulsive part of the sprint [28]
     and are clearly the most frequently injured muscle during sprinting [4]. The majority of
     hamstring muscle injuries occur while the athlete is running at maximal or close to maximal
     speeds [29] Many investigations have measured hamstring activity during sprinting with
     electromyographic (EMG), and found that the hamstrings are active from the middle of
     the swing to the final stance Some of these studies have reported that peak activity occurs
     during terminal swing [30], whereas others have found it to occur during stance [31]. Proof
     of the effort that these muscles exert in the sprint is that an increase in running speed of
     80–100% is linked with an increase in net hamstring muscle force and energy absorption of
     1.4 and 1.9 times, respectively [32]. However, this study took data from athletes running on
     a treadmill, and the mechanical properties of treadmill surfaces are different from those
     of the surfaces on which the athletes usually train and compete (e.g., artificial turf or an
     athletic track) [33]. This factor may influence running anatomy, so the results should be
     interpreted with caution.
           Regarding the CMJ results, the low thermal asymmetry hamstring group has signif-
     icantly higher values in the CMJ post-RSA, while in the calf and thigh groups, there are
     no significant differences in either CMJ pre- or CMJ post-RSA. Thus, the high thermal
     asymmetry hamstring group’s performance was similar to that of the low thermal asym-
     metry hamstring group before the RSA, and then its performance decreased in the CMJ
     post-RSA. This can be indicative of fatigue, as a decreased average CMJ jump height can
     indicate neuromuscular fatigue [34]. The reason why significant differences are only found
     in the high-asymmetry hamstring group (and not in the calf and thigh groups) may be that
     hamstrings are the most implicated and frequently injured group in sprinting [28], while
     calves and thighs seem to play a less crucial role in sprinting; therefore, asymmetry takes
     longer to turn into fatigue when performing an RSA test, as they are less implicated in
     this activity.
           Although the results of this study seem to provide evidence in terms of using and
     interpreting thermography to assess RSA and CMJ performance in elite football players,
     the results must be interpreted with caution, as certain limitations should be considered.
     First, thermography was carried out in just one session; applying thermography in a higher
     number of sessions would allow us to corroborate the results of the study. Second, a low
     asymmetry cut point was established, and settling a higher asymmetry cut point would
     probably show stronger correlations. Finally, the sample was very small, so future research
     should be carried out to look for evidence and to check whether these results apply to
     different genders, ages and competitive levels.
           From a practical point of view, if football coaches can access the thermographs of their
     players, they should focus especially on hamstrings (rather than calves and thighs) and

  "abstract": "The authors tested whether lower-limb skin temperature asymmetry measured by thermography related to repeated sprint performance and countermovement jump height in 20 male professional football players.   "tldr": "Hamstring temperature asymmetry showed a few links to sprint and jump results in 20 professional players, but the findings are preliminary. The study does not show that acting on these readings improves sprinting or jumping.",

 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Male Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Expert-opinion survey of chief medical officers from 15 European male professional clubs, with each club's hamstring injury burden over 2019/20 and 2020/21 used to split the clubs into 7 lower-burden and 8 higher-burden groups. Respondents suggested 21 modifiable hamstring risk factors and rated each on a 5-point importance scale. The top-rated factors were poor communication between medical and coaching staff (weighted average 3.7) and lack of regular high-speed training (3.6), and the higher-burden group rated coach leadership style, fatigue and player wellness as more important.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The findings are the perceived views of 15 medical officers rather than measured player-level or causal evidence, and the sample is small with only two seasons of injury data. The authors call the design an observational cohort study (prospective injury data, retrospective questionnaire), so it is coded that way, but the risk-factor ratings come from a single survey.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the ranking as proof that coaching style and communication cause hamstring injuries, when these are expert opinions from 15 clubs with no causal testing.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Ekstrand J, Ueblacker P, Van Zoest W, Verheijen R, Vanhecke B, van Wijk M, et al. Risk factors for hamstring muscle injury in male elite football: medical expert experience and conclusions from 15 European Champions League clubs. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. 2023;9:e001461.",
  "doi": "10.1136/bmjsem-2022-001461",
  "abstract": "Chief medical officers from 15 European professional clubs suggested and rated risk factors for hamstring injury, and their views were compared between clubs with lower and higher than average hamstring injury burden. Most of the 21 factors identified were extrinsic (coaching, team or club), led by poor communication between medical and coaching staff.",
  "tldr": "Club medical leaders mostly point to coaching, team and club factors, rather than player factors, as preventable causes of hamstring injury. Communication between medical and coaching staff and lack of high-speed training rank highest.",
  "methods": "Observational study in 15 clubs from the UEFA Elite Club Injury Study. Each club's chief medical officer answered an open question on preventable hamstring risk factors, then rated each of 21 factors on a 5-point importance scale. Clubs were divided by whether their hamstring injury burden was below or above the average across 2019/20 and 2020/21, and ratings were compared between the two groups.",
  "findings": "Lack of communication between medical and coaching staff had the highest weighted average (3.7), followed by lack of regular high-speed exposure in training (3.6). Of the 21 factors, 12 were extrinsic and 9 intrinsic, with mean importance 3.1 and 2.9. The higher-burden group rated coach leadership style much higher (3.3 vs 2.1), and rated fatigue (3.6 vs 2.6) and player wellness (3.0 vs 2.0) higher, while the lower-burden group rated lack of high-speed training higher (3.8 vs 3.5).",
  "limitations": "This is an opinion-based survey of 15 clubs with small groups (7 and 8) and two seasons of injury data, so causation cannot be inferred and the results may not generalize. Traumatic and gradual-onset hamstring injuries were pooled, and players were not asked for their views. The core ratings come from a one-time survey, not from measured exposures.",
  "practicalImplications": "Clubs could review how medical and coaching staff communicate about prevention, load and rehabilitation, since that was the most highly rated factor. The paper also points to training load, high-speed exposure and fatigue as things coaches control. These are the respondents' views rather than proven interventions, so clubs should track hamstring injuries in their own squad.",
  "athleteDev": "The paper names high-speed training exposure and load management as factors that performance and coaching staff control, so they are sensible areas to review with coaches. The lower-burden clubs rated lack of regular high-speed football as the highest factor in their group (3.8), but the ratings are opinions rather than tested effects.",
  "rtp": "Residual weakness after a previous hamstring injury was rated among the most important factors for individual players, and the authors note that insufficient strength and speed rehabilitation raises injury risk during high-speed play. The study tests no rehabilitation protocol and cannot set return-to-play criteria."

 "decision": "DEGRADED",
 "exclusionReason": "",

 "doiMissing": true,
 "identityCheck": "Title in the text (Selecting Metrics That Matter: Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and Injury Rehabilitation Testing) matches the filename; NSCA Strength and Conditioning Journal, 2023.",
 "confidence": "medium",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains": ["Monitoring & Technology", "Training & Performance", "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences": ["Performance", "Athletic Training", "Research & Analytics", "Rehabilitation"],
 "sports": ["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations": ["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Narrative review of the countermovement jump (CMJ), organized around three uses: performance profiling, neuromuscular fatigue monitoring and rehabilitation testing. It summarizes published associations with strength, speed and change-of-direction measures, and fatigue and recovery sensitivity, including one meta-analysis of 151 studies. Jump height and peak power track strength and speed well but change least after fatigue, while time-based and impulse metrics change most, and landing force and limb asymmetry are suggested for rehabilitation.",
 "screeningLimitations": "No systematic search or evidence grading is described, so the choice of cited studies reflects the authors' selection, and several points rest on single studies or the authors' experience. Table 2 and Table 3 use hypothetical data and Table 1 is adapted from one study of elite snowboard cross athletes, so these are illustrations rather than findings.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may treat the suggested metric choices as settled, when they are expert-led recommendations built on mixed, mostly single-study evidence.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2023,
  "citation": "Bishop C, Jordan M, Torres-Ronda L, et al. Selecting Metrics That Matter: Comparing the Use of the Countermovement Jump for Performance Profiling, Neuromuscular Fatigue Monitoring, and Injury Rehabilitation Testing. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2023.",
  "doi": "",
  "abstract": "This narrative review sets out which countermovement jump metrics to monitor depending on whether the test is used for performance profiling, neuromuscular fatigue monitoring or rehabilitation after injury. It argues that jump height and peak power link well to strength and speed, while time-based metrics are often more sensitive to fatigue.",
  "tldr": "Choose countermovement jump metrics to match the reason for testing. Jump height and power suit profiling, time-based and impulse metrics suit fatigue monitoring, and landing force and asymmetry may suit rehabilitation.",
  "methods": "Narrative review with three stated aims: an overview of common countermovement jump uses, practical guidance on which metrics to choose for each purpose, and how to judge real change against test error (coefficient of variation). It includes a schematic of metric choices and example tables. No search strategy is described.",
  "findings": "Jump height, peak force and peak power are consistently associated with strength, linear speed and change-of-direction measures. For fatigue, the authors cite a meta-analysis in which maximal jump height and peak power were not sensitive to fatigue (effect size -0.04 for both). Immediately after intense exercise, relative net impulse and flight time changed most, while time to peak power and flight time to contraction time ratio changed most over 24 to 72 hours. In cited injury work, previously injured players showed greater force asymmetries, while jump height did not differ significantly.",
  "limitations": "There is no systematic search or formal evidence grading, so conclusions depend on the authors' selection of studies. Tables 2 and 3 use hypothetical data for illustration, Table 1 is adapted from a single study, and the authors acknowledge that some recommendations are anecdotal.",
  "practicalImplications": "Decide why you are testing before choosing metrics. For profiling, track jump height, peak force and peak power. For fatigue, add time-based metrics such as time to peak power, and check any change against the athlete's own coefficient of variation before calling it real. For rehabilitation, consider landing force and limb asymmetry alongside test-retest error.",
  "athleteDev": "For profiling, jump height, peak force and peak power are consistently linked to strength and speed, so they justify their place in an athlete profile. The review also suggests adding time-based metrics and keeping test instructions consistent so that changes reflect fitness rather than a different jump strategy.",
  "rtp": "The review says jump height and power may matter less in rehabilitation, while landing force and limb asymmetry may reveal residual deficits. It gives no pass criteria or validated cut-offs, so it cannot tell staff when an athlete is ready to return to sport."
 }
}
